dailyRead: Two things changed at Friday's close and the more important one is a change of reason rather than of direction. All week this file has treated the December 9 Fed meeting as a question of size, and that question has now closed: Waller's stated condition for considering a half-point was a hot October inflation print, Thursday's producer number was below forecast at the margin, he has himself said he leans to a quarter-point, and CME-based pricing still carries only about 13% on 50bp against roughly 87% on 25bp. What has replaced it is bigger. Polymarket now prices a January hike at 57.5%, up 39 points in a single week, and one OIS-based tracker carries about 86 basis points of tightening over twelve months, which is three and a half quarter-point moves. Logan was explicit on Friday that the committee needs at least two more 25 basis point increases and that it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter; Daly said there are lots of options for December and pointed at persistent services inflation while saying there is no urgency; Collins said the direction is clear without committing to size or pace; and Jefferson, speaking at San Diego, said he is taking his policy cues from inflation and that October's data was consistent with well-above-target inflation. That is a committee arguing about how far, not whether. Price agreed: the dollar index closed at 103.411, up 0.23% on the day, a 19-month high, and MUFG has it as the best G10 performer of the week, up against all seven majors - biggest gain against the franc, smallest against the kiwi. TradingEconomics carries the US 10-year at 5.15% into the close, the 30-year at 5.47%, the 2-year at 4.86% and, the number that matters most for metals, the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.90%, up 5.6 basis points on the day. The second change is one this file had entirely missed and should not have. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive and from its board around November 11 to 12 after the board opened an independent investigation into his conduct; the chief financial officer, Colette Kress, is interim chief executive. Nvidia fell 4.34% on Thursday and another 2.01% on Friday, closing below a 4 trillion dollar market capitalisation for the first time since July 2025, with AMD down 8.8%, Broadcom 4.9% and Qualcomm 2.6% on Friday. That matters here for three reasons. It explains the metals: investinglive attributes part of Friday's slide to margin-call selling out of the tech rout rather than rates alone, and the signature is unmistakable - silver fell 2.59% to 48.72 and back under the round 50 dollar level while gold rose 0.14% to 3,881.75, holding just above Thursday's one-year low settlement near 3,885. It explains the European tape, where Infineon lost 4.29% and ASML 2.76% while the DAX itself closed almost unchanged at 26,749.95. And most usefully it tells us what kind of risk-off this is: a genuine equity scare that bid neither gold nor the franc, only the dollar. That last point is the correction this file owes. Yesterday the argument was that the oil bounce had re-bid the haven and the franc therefore came up from minus two to minus one. The oil bounce was real and it held - Brent closed 95.84 and WTI 88.56 - but the franc then lost ground to six of the seven other majors on Friday, with USD/CHF up 0.43%, and it was the dollar's biggest weekly gain of the board. The trigger arrived and the price did not follow, so that upgrade is on probation rather than confirmed; what keeps CHF at minus one rather than back at minus two is that the structural case is genuinely two-sided, with EUR/CHF having fallen 3.1% in October for the franc's best month in five years, Swiss headline CPI at a near three-year high of 1.5%, and ING still expecting more interest in the currency. The oil picture itself got structurally worse and tactically quieter, which is an awkward combination. Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has set seven conditions for talks and Tehran is waiting on a US reply; Iran has said the Strait will never return to the way it worked before the war and claims an understanding with Oman over managing it. The straits.live tracker has the waterway closed on day 258 and cites IMF PortWatch at three transits on November 8 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, while an Oilprice analysis argues regional flows have recovered to near pre-war levels - the two cannot both be right, which is itself the reason USOIL is a range. Crude barely moved on Friday, Brent plus 0.02% and WTI minus 0.20%, and the gas spike that drove yesterday's sterling and euro upgrades has partly unwound: UK gas fell 1.58% to 227.01 pence from the 236.10 this file carried, EU gas 1.41% to 90.955 euros from 94.74. Sterling stays at plus one but the load-bearing leg has moved from gas to Wednesday's October CPI, which the Bank's own November Monetary Policy Report puts at 3.73% headline with core at 2.9% and services at 3.9%, against a September headline of 3.5%. On the euro, one correction on pricing: this file carried a 94% to 95% probability for the December 17 ECB hike and that number was not re-verifiable today. What is verifiable is that all 71 economists in the Reuters poll expect a quarter-point to 2.75% and that most of them call it the last of the cycle, while market-based estimates I could confirm sit in a 67% to 84% range depending on source and date. The unanimity is the stronger fact and the euro stays at plus one, but the 'final hike' consensus is what now caps the Euro Stoxx bank leg and is why EU50 comes off its long. The yen deserves the last word because the framing changed rather than the price. USD/JPY closed 159.707, down 0.08%, after touching 160.19 in Tokyo, the weakest in about two and a half months - and yet the yen gained against all seven majors on Friday, with AUD/JPY down 0.62% and CHF/JPY down 0.52%, because the equity rout bid it. Set against that, two facts cut the other way from yesterday's read. This file called 160 an official floor; it is not. Japan has named no automatic level, the record 27.1 trillion yen already spent did not hold the line, and one analysis puts the likely trigger nearer 163, the July level. And Monday at 01:50 brings Q3 GDP that the Reuters poll of 16 economists sees at 0.3% annualised from 1.4%, with private consumption down 0.2% for its first fall in seven quarters and net external demand subtracting about 0.4 points. A currency that is weak on price, strongest on the day, hawkish on policy and facing a dovish growth print is the definition of mixed, so JPY stays at zero - but nothing on this board should be long USD/JPY at 159.7 and nothing should be short it either.

today.headline: The half-point died and the path replaced it: January hike odds reached 57.5%, up 39 points in a week, and the index closed at a 19-month high of 103.411
today.read: This is the most important change on the board and it is a change of reason rather than direction. The size question is closed - Waller's condition for a half-point was a hot October print, he has said he leans to 25bp himself, and pricing still carries only about 13% on 50bp against roughly 87% on 25bp. What the market has started paying for instead is duration of tightening: Polymarket has January at 57.5% from about 18% a week ago, and one OIS-based tracker carries about 86 basis points over twelve months, three and a half quarter-point moves. Friday's roster of speakers is consistent with that and not with a bigger December. Logan was the clearest - the committee needs at least two more 25 basis point increases, and it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter. Daly said there are lots of options for December, pointed at persistent services inflation and said there is no urgency. Collins said the direction is clear without committing to size or pace. Jefferson, at San Diego, said he is taking his policy cues from inflation and that October's data was consistent with well-above-target inflation, having been part of the 10 to 2 October majority that chose to wait. Reports on Bowman conflict and are not reliable enough to use. Price confirms rather than leads: the index closed 103.411, plus 0.23% on the day and plus 4.14% on the year, and MUFG makes it the best G10 performer of the week, up against all seven majors with the biggest gain against the franc and the smallest against the kiwi. TradingEconomics has the 10-year at 5.15% into the close, the 30-year at 5.47%, the 20-year at 5.53%, the 2-year at 4.86% and the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.90%, up 5.6 basis points. The score stays at plus two rather than going to plus three for a specific reason: a 0.23% day is not an upgrade, the whole board is already positioned for this, and Tuesday's retail sales at a plus 0.2% forecast is the first real two-way risk in a week. The honest statement of the thesis is that the dollar is no longer capped by resistance and no longer carries a half-point tail - it is paid by a path that still has 42 percentage points of January to price.

today.headline: The yen gained against all seven majors on Friday and still closed near its weakest in two and a half months, and 160 turns out not to be an official floor
today.read: Two corrections to yesterday's read, pulling in opposite directions, which is why the score does not move. The first is bearish. This file called 160 an official floor; it is not one. Japan has never named an automatic intervention level, the record 27.1 trillion yen already spent did not hold the line, the yen reached 160.19 in Tokyo on Friday anyway, and one analysis puts the likely trigger nearer 163 - the July level - rather than 160. That is a materially weaker backstop than the one this file described, and it was the single thing holding the yen at zero rather than lower. The second is bullish and arrived from outside Japan. In Friday's equity rout the yen was the strongest currency on the board, gaining against all seven majors: AUD/JPY minus 0.62%, CHF/JPY minus 0.52%, NZD/JPY minus 0.46%, EUR/JPY minus 0.37%, GBP/JPY minus 0.26%, CAD/JPY minus 0.17%, USD/JPY minus 0.08% to 159.707. The Nvidia unwind bid the yen and did not bid gold or the franc, which tells you the yen is still the market's reflex haven even at 160. MUFG's weekly ranking has it outperforming most of G10 with only the kiwi and the euro ahead of it, so the framing of the yen as the week's weakest major - which this file has used - was wrong. Policy is unchanged and still hawkish: 1.25% now, a Reuters poll majority on 1.50% at December 18, wage growth 4.6% and the fastest here, September CPI 2.1% with core at 2.1%, and the October 30 judgement that underlying inflation met 2% for the first time since 2013. The near risk is Monday at 01:50, where Q3 preliminary GDP is seen at 0.3% annualised from 1.4% by a Reuters poll of 16, with private consumption down 0.2% for its first fall in seven quarters and net external demand subtracting about 0.4 points. Weak on price, strongest on the day, hawkish on policy, with a dovish growth print in a few hours and a softer intervention backstop than advertised: that is zero, and it is the reason nothing on this board is long or short USD/JPY.

today.headline: The worst G10 performer of the month at minus 3.4%, and copper fell another 1.67% to confirm it
today.read: The Aussie was the biggest mover on Friday as well as the weakest major on the month, with AUD/USD down 0.54% to 0.67714, and the external check this file uses on it moved the same way: copper closed 6.0795, down 1.67% on the day and 8.05% on the month. That matters because a genuine Australian demand story would appear in copper before it appeared in the currency, and it keeps not appearing. The domestic position is unchanged and remains the clearest dovish pivot on this board: the November 3 statement dropped the line about raising further if needed, the hike passed 6 to 3 with the three dissenters wanting a pause, and Westpac reads 4.85% as likely the cycle peak. The tension is that this is also the highest inflation here - 4.3% for Q3 with core at 3.6% - and a labour market that shed 39,329 jobs in September with unemployment at 4.7% is what lets the Bank live with it. What makes the coming week different is density: the November minutes Tuesday at 02:30, the Q3 wage price index Wednesday at 02:30, and October employment Thursday at 02:30 with a plus 27,500 forecast against September's fall and unemployment seen steady. Three chances to break a minus one in a currency with no meeting until December 8, which is exactly why the conviction on the Aussie shorts stays at medium rather than going higher despite the widest score spreads on the board. Minutes that restore conditional hiking language would squeeze AUD/NZD and EUR/AUD hardest.

today.headline: The worst G10 performer of the week, and the oil-bounce trigger this file named for a franc bid arrived without the bid
today.read: This is the correction that matters most for conviction, because it is a test this file set in advance and then failed. Yesterday the franc came up from minus two to minus one on the explicit argument that a collapsed Iran negotiation with the Strait still blocked would bring haven flows back and that a central bank which had stepped away from selling francs could not cap them. The premise held: Brent closed 95.84, keeping the bounce, and Iran hardened rather than softened, with Ghalibaf's seven conditions and the statement that the Strait will never return to pre-war operation. The conclusion did not. The franc lost ground to six of the seven other majors on Friday - USD/CHF plus 0.43% to 0.83894, CAD/CHF plus 0.33%, GBP/CHF plus 0.26%, EUR/CHF plus 0.14% to 0.92476, NZD/CHF plus 0.05%, and only AUD/CHF minus 0.12% the other way - and Babypips has the dollar's largest weekly gain of all seven coming against it. More tellingly, Friday's equity rout was a real risk-off event and it bid the yen and the dollar while the franc went down with the Aussie. So the upgrade is on probation, not confirmed. What keeps it at minus one rather than back at minus two is that the structural side is genuinely two-sided and not a courtesy: EUR/CHF fell 3.1% in October, the franc's largest monthly gain against the euro in five years, October CPI at 1.5% is a near three-year high that has reinforced some expectations of a more hawkish SNB, and ING still expects more interest in the currency with downside risks to its EUR/CHF forecasts. Against all of that, core CPI is 0.5% and producer prices are about minus 0.2% y/y, so the headline is energy and the policy rate stays at zero through the December 10 assessment. The franc short remains the board's best-performing dollar expression and its least convincing cross expression.

today.headline: The gas spike that drove yesterday's upgrade partly unwound, so Wednesday's CPI at the Bank's own 3.73% forecast is now the load-bearing leg
today.read: Sterling stays at plus one but the reason has shifted and it is worth being precise about which leg is now carrying it. Yesterday the upgrade rested on two things: that Bailey's condition for November not being the last hike - an unresolved Middle East conflict - was being met, and that UK gas at 236.10 pence was plus 11.24% on the week and the sharpest energy input in G10. The first leg strengthened: Iran has said the Strait will never return to pre-war operation and set seven conditions for talks, which is the opposite of resolution. The second leg weakened. UK gas closed 227.01 pence, down 1.58% on the day, giving back a meaningful part of that spike, though it is still plus 5.09% on the month. Price was mid-pack rather than strong - GBP/USD minus 0.17% to 1.32132, though sterling did gain on the euro with EUR/GBP minus 0.13% to 0.83424. What now decides the December 17 meeting arrives Wednesday at 09:00, and the number to hold in mind is the Bank's own: the November Monetary Policy Report projects October headline CPI at 3.73% with core at 2.9% and services at 3.9%, against a September headline of 3.5% and core of 2.8%. A print at or above that forecast makes a second consecutive hike the base case and takes sterling to plus two; a miss hands the December doves the argument they lost when September GDP came in at plus 0.2% against a flat forecast. Tuesday's labour market report at 09:00 is the other input, with the Report expecting unemployment to average 4.8% into Q4 against the 4.7% currently carried. MPC member Greene speaks today at 13:00, the first MPC voice since the oil reversal.

today.headline: A 19-month low at 1.10236, and the December hike that all 71 economists expect is also the one most of them call the last
today.read: Two things to separate here, because they point different ways for the currency and the equity index. The currency keeps plus one on the strongest piece of evidence available anywhere on this board: every one of the 71 economists in the November 10 to 12 Reuters poll expects a quarter-point to 2.75% on December 17. That is unanimity, and it is why the euro holds its rank even as EUR/USD closed 1.10236, down 0.28% and a 19-month low, and minus 5.13% on the year. The correction owed is on market pricing. This file carried 94% to 95% for the December hike and that figure was not re-verifiable today; the market-based estimates I could confirm run roughly 67% to 84% depending on source and date, so the economists' consensus is the firmer fact and the probability claim has to come down. The macro case is intact but narrow: October HICP at 4.0% is a three-year high while core sits steady at 2.5%, which makes this an energy-driven move rather than a domestic one - and that is precisely why most of those 71 economists see December as the end of the cycle. Growth is adequate at 0.4% q/q and 1.3% y/y for Q3, and Friday's flash Q3 employment printed 0.0% q/q against a plus 0.2% forecast, down from plus 0.1%, which is the one genuinely new macro reading on this board today. The Bund closed 3.38%, a two-week high, against a US 10-year at 5.15%, so the rate gap still runs against the euro by 177 basis points. Gas cooled - EU gas minus 1.41% to 90.955 euros from the 94.74 carried yesterday - which removes some of the inflation impulse the hike is answering. Final October CPI Wednesday at 12:00, the October meeting accounts November 26 at 14:30.

today.headline: Flat into Monday's CPI, with crude quiet at 88.56 and nothing domestic yet earning the upgrade
today.read: The loonie did almost nothing on Friday - USD/CAD plus 0.08% to 1.42694, CAD/JPY minus 0.17%, CAD/CHF plus 0.33% - and that is the correct behaviour for a currency whose next move is entirely in one print. Monday at 15:30 brings October CPI at a plus 0.3% m/m and 3.2% y/y forecast against September's 3.1%, with the Bank's core measures averaging around 2.0% to 2.2%. The reason CAD sits at zero and not higher is unchanged and worth repeating: it came off minus one purely because crude stopped falling, which is an absence of a negative rather than a positive, and crude has now gone quiet rather than extended - WTI closed 88.56, down 0.20% on the day and 6.87% on the month, Brent 95.84 and plus 0.02%. The domestic picture gives the Bank no help: unemployment rose to 6.7% in October for a six-month high, employment fell 4,700 for a third consecutive decline, growth is 1.1% y/y and the policy rate is 2.50% after the October 28 rise. A firm print makes the December 9 decision live and earns plus one; a soft one restores the dovish case and sends it back to minus one. This is the cleanest binary on the board next week and it lands first alongside Japan's GDP.

today.headline: Still the best non-dollar major of the week with nothing new to price before the December 9 Statement
today.read: The kiwi gave back 0.38% to 0.55250 on Friday in a session where the dollar took something from everyone, but the weekly picture is unchanged and favourable: MUFG and Babypips both have the dollar's smallest weekly gain coming against the kiwi, making it the best-performing non-dollar major of the week, and it gained on the Aussie again with AUD/NZD down 0.17% to 1.22537. The case is unchanged because nothing touched it. The December 9 Monetary Policy Statement at 03:00 carries a hike priced near 75%, against Q3 CPI at 3.7% with core at 3.2% and the Bank's own forecast of roughly 4.4% for Q4 - a path the Bank expects to get worse before it improves, and one that higher fuel prices feed directly, which is why the Iran reversal is a kiwi positive rather than a negative. The counterweight is the weakest labour market on this board: unemployment at 5.7% for Q3 is the highest since 2016 and employment fell 0.1% on the quarter, which is why October's hold was 4 to 3 rather than unanimous and why this is plus one rather than plus two. There is no New Zealand data of consequence for three weeks, so the kiwi will trade the Australian calendar - minutes Tuesday, wages Wednesday, jobs Thursday - and the dollar leg. That makes AUD/NZD the purest way to hold it.

Minutes that restore conditional hiking language are what would squeeze AUD/NZD and EUR/AUD hardest, and they are the first of three Australian tests this week.

At 09:00 and the most consequential release of the week for this board. The Bank's own November Monetary Policy Report projects headline at 3.73% with core at 2.9% and services at 3.9%, against a September headline of 3.5% and core of 2.8%. At or above that forecast, a second consecutive hike on December 17 becomes the base case and sterling goes to plus two; a clear miss hands the doves the argument they lost on growth.

catalysts.event: FOMC minutes from the October 28 meeting
catalysts.note: At 21:00. The meeting held at 3.75% to 4.00% by 10 votes to 2, with Cook and Hammack dissenting in favour of a quarter-point rise. It predates the October CPI print, so the value is in the distribution of views rather than in guidance - specifically whether the hawkish chorus of Friday's speakers represents the committee or a wing of it.

catalysts.event: Australia Q3 wage price index and euro-area final October CPI
catalysts.note: Australian wages at 02:30, the second of three Australian tests and the one that speaks most directly to whether 4.85% is really the peak. Euro-area final October CPI at 12:00 against a 4.0% flash with core at 2.5%; a material upward revision would reopen the argument for an ECB path beyond December, which is the leg EU50 needs.

At 02:30, forecast plus 27,500 against September's 39,329 fall, with unemployment seen steady at 4.7%. The last and largest of the three Australian tests, and the clearest single way the board's widest score spread - plus two against minus one - gets narrowed before the December 8 meeting.

At 01:30. September came in at 2.1% with core also 2.1%, and the Bank judged on October 30 that underlying inflation had met 2% for the first time since 2013. Read together with Monday's GDP this is the pair that decides whether December 18 is a hike or a hold.

catalysts.event: UK retail sales and euro-area consumer confidence
catalysts.note: UK retail sales at 09:00, with the BRC monitor having shown a slowdown before Black Friday, plus the public finances and a Moody's UK credit review. Euro-area flash consumer confidence at 17:00 and the Q3 negotiated wage indicator, the latter relevant to whether December really is the ECB's last.

At 14:30. The record of the October 29 hold, read for how close the Council already was to moving - and more importantly now, for any sign of a path beyond December. All 71 economists in the Reuters poll expect a quarter-point on December 17 and most call it the last of the cycle; accounts that contradict that are what would restore the EU50 long.

At 05:30. Westpac reads this as a pause to assess and calls 4.85% likely the peak of the cycle after the November statement dropped its conditional hiking language and the hike passed over three dissents.

catalysts.event: Fed decision and projections, RBNZ Statement, Bank of Canada
catalysts.note: Three decisions in one day: the RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement at 03:00 priced near 75%, the Bank of Canada at 16:45, and the Fed with new projections at 21:00 where a quarter-point is roughly 87% to 91% priced and a half-point about 13%. With the half-point effectively dead, the Fed's projections - how many moves the committee pencils for 2027 - are now the tradeable part rather than the decision. The single biggest day on this horizon.

At 10:30. A hike is not expected and the conditional forecast assumes zero through 2028, so the tradeable content is whether the Bank restores the intervention threat it eased in September. This matters more now that the franc has been the worst G10 performer of the week and did not attract a bid in a genuine equity rout.

catalysts.event: ECB and Bank of England decisions
catalysts.note: The BoE at 14:00 and the ECB at 15:15. All 71 economists in the Reuters poll expect the ECB to reach 2.75% and most call it the final hike; verifiable market pricing runs roughly 67% to 84%. The BoE is a genuine coin flip that Wednesday's CPI will largely settle, with Bailey's condition for a further rise being that the conflict is not resolved.

At 05:00. A Reuters poll majority expects 1.50% and DBS argues trend growth near 0.8% annualised and sticky inflation justify it, though dovish Bank commentary has taken some of that expectation back. Intervention is the nearer risk than the meeting - and 160 is not the trigger, with one analysis putting the likely line nearer 163.

catalysts.event: Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and the stalled US negotiation
catalysts.note: The dominant variable on this board and it hardened this week rather than resolving. Trump said the United States does not need a deal because it already has Iran's money and its Strait; Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has set seven conditions for talks with Tehran awaiting a US reply; and Iran has said the Strait will never return to pre-war operation while claiming an understanding with Oman. The straits.live tracker has it closed on day 258 citing IMF PortWatch at three transits on November 8 against an 85-a-day baseline, while an Oilprice analysis says regional flows have recovered to near pre-war levels. Crude went nowhere on Friday regardless, Brent plus 0.02% and WTI minus 0.20%.

catalysts.event: Nvidia leadership vacuum and the AI equity unwind
catalysts.note: New to this file and it should have been here sooner. Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and from the board around November 11 to 12 after the board opened an independent investigation into his conduct; CFO Colette Kress is interim chief executive. The stock fell 4.34% on Thursday and 2.01% on Friday, closing below a 4 trillion dollar market capitalisation for the first time since July 2025, with AMD down 8.8%, Broadcom 4.9% and Qualcomm 2.6%. The FX relevance is specific: this is a risk-off that bids the yen and the dollar and bids neither gold nor the franc, and the forced selling out of it is what broke silver back under 50 dollars.

geopolitics: The oil transmission chain held its new direction this week and then stopped transmitting, which is a more awkward state than either escalation or de-escalation. The structural picture clearly worsened. Trump's line that the United States does not need a deal because it already has Iran's money and its Strait has now been joined by a hardening on the Iranian side: the parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has set seven conditions for negotiations with Washington and Tehran is waiting on a US reply, while Iran has stated that the Strait will never return to the way it operated before the war and claims to have reached an understanding with Oman over managing the waterway. The physical read remains contested in a way that matters for position sizing: the straits.live tracker has the Strait closed on day 258 and cites IMF PortWatch at three transits on November 8 against a pre-crisis baseline of 85 a day, while an Oilprice analysis argues crude flows from Hormuz and the wider region have recovered to near pre-war levels. Those two cannot both be right, and the honest consequence is that USOIL stays a range rather than becoming a long. Price agreed with the ambiguity rather than with the rhetoric: Brent closed 95.84 and plus 0.02%, WTI 88.56 and minus 0.20%, both still down on the month at 9.64% and 6.87%, with OPEC+ output surging and US inventories having built roughly 9 million barrels. The FX consequences divide into one that strengthened, one that cooled and one that failed outright. Strengthened: sterling's hawkish leg, because Bailey's condition for the November hike not being the last is that the conflict is not resolved, and a counterparty saying the Strait will never reopen as before is the opposite of resolution. Cooled: the energy-inflation channel that made that argument concrete in both Britain and the euro area. UK gas closed 227.01 pence, down 1.58% on the day from the 236.10 this file carried, and EU gas 90.955 euros, down 1.41% from 94.74 - so both the sterling and euro upgrades now rest on next week's inflation prints rather than on live energy costs. Failed outright: the franc. The mechanism this file set out in advance was that a collapsed negotiation with the Strait still blocked would bring war-driven haven flows back, and that an SNB which eased its intervention threat in September could not cap them. The premise held and the bid never came - the franc was the worst G10 performer of the week, lost ground to six of the seven other majors on Friday, and most tellingly failed to attract any bid at all during a genuine equity rout. That rout is the week's second geopolitical-grade event and it came from corporate governance rather than from a government: Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia and its board left the largest company in the AI complex without a permanent chief executive and below a 4 trillion dollar market capitalisation. The FX signature of that session is worth committing to memory because it is likely to repeat. The yen was bid and was the strongest currency on the board. The dollar was bid. Gold rose 0.14% and did nothing. The franc fell. This is a risk-off in which the haven function has consolidated into the yen and the dollar, which means the reciprocal risk has changed too: a genuine Iran de-escalation would now hit sterling and the euro through the inflation channel and would help the franc short rather than breaking it, while a deepening AI unwind would break every yen cross on this board at once. Those are two different tail events pulling in two different directions, and neither is priced.
